title: Amazon MQ
description: Learn how Amazon MQ provides managed ActiveMQ and RabbitMQ brokers for traditional message-oriented middleware workloads.

data.text: Amazon MQ is a managed message broker service for Apache ActiveMQ and RabbitMQ. If you have existing applications using these brokers, Amazon MQ lets you migrate to the cloud without rewriting code.
ActiveMQ is a mature, JMS-based message broker supporting queues and topics. RabbitMQ is a lightweight broker that implements the AMQP protocol and is popular for microservices communication.

data.title: When to Use Amazon MQ
items: **Migration from on-premises** — lift-and-shift applications already using ActiveMQ or RabbitMQ
**Legacy applications** — apps that require JMS or AMQP APIs
**Message ordering** — strict ordering is required across multiple consumers
**Message persistence** — all messages are durably stored to disk

data.text: Amazon MQ offers two deployment modes: single-instance brokers for development and test, and active/standby brokers for production. Active/standby brokers replicate data synchronously across two Availability Zones for high availability.
Amazon MQ is best when you need a traditional message broker with JMS or AMQP. SQS and SNS are serverless, cloud-native alternatives that are simpler and more scalable for new applications.

cards.title: Amazon SQS
cards.description: Fully managed queue for cloud-native applications.
cons: No message ordering in standard queues

cards.title: Amazon SNS
cards.description: Fully managed pub/sub for cloud-native applications.
cons: No persistent message storage by default

cards.title: Amazon MQ
cards.description: Managed ActiveMQ or RabbitMQ for traditional middleware.

data.title: Choose Amazon MQ Wisely
data.text: Amazon MQ is for migrating legacy applications. For new applications, prefer SQS and SNS unless you specifically need JMS or AMQP compatibility.

terms.definition: An intermediary that routes, stores, and delivers messages between producers and consumers.
An open-source message broker supporting JMS queues and topics.
An open-source message broker implementing the AMQP protocol, popular for microservices.
A high-availability Amazon MQ deployment with synchronous replication across two AZs.

data.title: Deploy an Amazon MQ Broker
data.description: Create an Amazon MQ ActiveMQ broker in the AWS console and connect a client application to it.
steps: Open the Amazon MQ console and create a new broker
Choose ActiveMQ and select the active/standby deployment type
Configure a username and password for the broker
Once the broker is available, copy the WebSocket URL
Connect a simple Java or Python client to publish and consume messages
data.expectedOutcome: You will have a running Amazon MQ broker and a working client that can send and receive messages.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Amazon MQ provides managed ActiveMQ and RabbitMQ brokers
Active/standby brokers provide high availability across AZs
Use Amazon MQ for legacy migrations; use SQS/SNS for new cloud-native apps
JMS and AMQP compatibility lets you reuse existing application code
data.takeaway: Amazon MQ bridges the gap between traditional middleware and the cloud, but SQS and SNS are usually the better choice for new applications.
